title: Intelligence engineering
summary: Plan an AI system around a useful task, then decide how to show that it works.
detail:
Start with a task someone needs to complete, such as finding the policy for a customer’s product. Follow their request through the application’s API, the interface used by other software. Retrieval finds relevant source passages; generation produces an answer; tools let the application perform other operations.

Each handoff needs a contract: what it accepts, what it returns and what happens when it fails. Select the parts your task needs, then build an evaluation plan: the cases and checks that would show the design works. Ask what a wrong answer or failed action would cost the user.
failures: A polished demonstration has no evidence from the tasks real users need.

title: API & gateway
summary: Define how other software asks your application to do a task.
detail:
An application programming interface (API) specifies how software sends a request and receives a result. A gateway receives calls and routes them to a service; it may also enforce shared limits. The application must still decide what the request means, who may perform it, how long it can run and what result to return.

An application API serves the user’s task. A model API asks a model to generate output. A tool gateway exposes operations an agent may request. Identify which interface you are designing before choosing its checks.
inputs: Request with a verified caller identity
The caller’s organisation or account, and the requested task
outputs: Measurements and events tied to the request
failures: One organisation or account can read another’s restricted data.
An incorrect answer is treated as valid because the web response reports success.
Repeated attempts create duplicate changes or messages.

title: Request & response contract
summary: Decide what a successful response actually means.
detail:
A request and response contract tells callers which fields to send and what each possible result means. Validate inputs by checking their required fields, types and allowed values. Return consistent error categories so the caller can respond. Test permission checks separately from the model.

JSON is a structured text format for values such as strings, lists and objects. A response can match its JSON schema, the rules for those fields, while containing a false answer. Test both the structure and the task result.
inputs: Rules for request fields and values
Rules for who may perform the action
outputs: Response with defined fields and value types
Defined errors and what the caller should do
failures: A missing value becomes an empty string, hiding the difference between absent and blank.
A request has no limit on size, work or duration.
Generated text is executed as though it were trusted program code.

title: Model routing & budgets
summary: Choose where a request runs and what it may consume.
detail:
Routing selects the model deployment that will handle a request. A provider operates a model service; a deployment is the configured place where your requests run. Set limits on response time and tokens, the pieces of text a model processes and generates.

Record the provider, model revision, prompt instructions and retrieval settings for each comparison. A fallback is an alternative used when the first route fails. Test it on the same tasks: it may support different tools, produce different answers or send data to a different location. Ask which alternatives are permitted before enabling them.
inputs: Limits on response time and input/output tokens
outputs: Defined alternative route or explicit error
failures: The selected model changes without a recorded revision.
Repeated retries across services multiply the incoming load.
Data reaches a region that the project has not permitted.
